title: Reducing Self-Criticism Through a Virtual Reality Intervention: A Randomized Controlled Trial
summary: Many people experience persistent negative thoughts about themselves, such as harsh self-criticism or feelings of being unworthy. These thoughts often develop early in life and can contribute to emotional problems like depression, anxiety, or eating disorders. Traditional psychological therapies use imagination-based techniques to help people change these patterns, but some individuals find it difficult to vividly imagine and emotionally connect with these exercises. This study investigates whether a Virtual Reality–based therapeutic exercise can reduce self-criticism more effectively than a neutral Virtual Reality experience in adults with elevated self-critical thinking. Participants will be randomly assigned to one of two groups. One group will receive a single Virtual Reality session that guides them through a therapeutic self-dialogue exercise designed to reduce self-criticism. The control group will spend the same amount of time in a neutral Virtual Reality environment without therapeutic content. Self-report questionnaires will be completed before the session, immediately afterward, and four weeks later to assess changes in self-criticism and related psychological outcomes.
conditions: Participants (aged 18–64 years) with subclinical levels of self-criticism

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Forms of SelfCriticizing/Attacking and Self-Reassuring Scale (FSCRS:.  >20 on the ‘Inadequate Self’- scale (range 0–36)
Exclusion criteria:
Participants who score >0 on item 9 of the BDI-II (suicidal ideation), are 
currently under psychological treatment,or have taken prescribed medication or undergone a change in medication dosage within the last 3 months will be excluded, as well as limited or no 3D perception, diagnosed with epilepsy or a tendency toward epileptic seizures,  problems with binocular vision, pregnancy, heart disease or any other physical ilness.
